$comment: The workbench guide in the docs (docs/tools/workbench/…, tool-docs.mjs): one short page per area. The first page is the overview (its what/when comes from data/tools.json; it also shows the labelled screenshot from tourparts.json and the list of these pages). Per page: slug (under docs/), nav (its name in the list), title, desc (one line: the page's description and its line in lists), intro (what this part is, a sentence or two), shots (gallery screenshots, without -light/-dark; captions from the start page's gallery, or [name, caption] for one that isn't in it), sections (h + md: how it works, short), keys (action ids from keyactions.ts: the page's shortcut table), tips (ids from tips.ts: shown under "Tips from the workbench"), said (tips the page's own text already covers, so they aren't repeated; a test checks every workbench tip is in one page's tips or said, or in skipTips). In text: `code`, **bold**, {key:<action id>} for a shortcut, a lone key in backticks (`F8`), [links](https://…), (@guide:<page id>) for another page here, (@site:<path>) for a page of the site, (@docs:<slug>) for a docs page. Lines starting with "- " are a list, with "1. " numbered steps. Write it the way you'd explain it to someone on Discord (AGENTS.md, Conventions).

pages.title: Workbench
pages.desc: What the workbench is, where everything is, and a guide to each part.

sections.md:
1. [Open the workbench](@site:). There's already a template handler in the editor, so you have something to play with.
2. On your first visit it asks two things. Do you want guidance (**Guide me**) or would you rather get on with it (**I write code**), and which layout do you prefer. Both only set defaults, and you can change everything later in Settings.
3. After that a short tour points out the parts of the screen. If you skip it, **Take the tour** in the menu brings it back.

Your handlers are kept in the browser you're using. Each one gets a tab, and they're still there next time.

pages.title: Writing code in the workbench
pages.desc: Suggestions, hover docs, the Docs tab, Lines and the editing keys.
pages.intro: The left side is a code editor that knows the handler API. While you type it suggests names that really exist and shows their docs, and for most options it can drop a working example into your code.

sections.h: Suggestions and docs while you type
sections.md:
- Type `.` after `Game`, `Context` or `Nucleus` to see what exists there, with the docs for each name. {key:suggest} opens the same list anywhere.
- Hover a name to read its docs. Inside a call, {key:parameterHints} tells you what goes where.
- After a `=` the editor offers the values that option accepts.

**Docs**, on the right, is the full reference. Search it for an option, a `Context` member or a Nucleus value, or leave the search empty and browse. The empty view also lists the names Hub handlers use most, which is a decent place to start.

Most entries come with an example, and **Insert into handler** puts it in the right spot for you. An option goes with your other options. A call goes inside `Game.Play`.

sections.h: Lines, if you'd rather click than type
sections.md: **Lines** ({key:lines}) lists every name a handler can use, next to the code. Click one and it's inserted. Names your handler already sets show their current value.

Put the cursor on a line and press {key:explainLine}. You get the line in plain words, the docs for the names on it, and anything Check has to say about it. It's handy when you're reading someone else's handler.
{key:format} tidies indentation and spacing. It never moves anything to another line. Nucleus reads handlers line by line, and we don't want formatting to change what it sees.

pages.title: Check: problems and fixes
pages.desc: How Check finds problems and how to fix them.
pages.intro: Check looks for things Nucleus Co-op would reject or quietly get wrong, and it does that while you type. Each problem comes with the reason it matters, and usually with a fix.
shots: Fix all shows a before and after. Nothing changes until you accept it.

sections.md:
You'll see a problem in three places. There's a squiggle under the code, a marker beside the line number, and a card in the **Check** tab on the right. The card tells you what's wrong, why Nucleus cares, and how to fix it.

Errors mean the handler won't work. Warnings and hints won't stop it, but they're usually worth reading.

- For one line, press {key:quickFix} (`Alt+Enter` works too) and pick a fix.
- **Fix all** does every automatic fix in one go. It shows you a before and after first.
- Some problems need you to decide something. Those stay in the list, with the options you have.
- If you've set up an AI, [Fix with AI](@guide:ai) can try the ones that are left.

Check doesn't stop at the code. It also looks at the files that ship with the handler. If you link your game's install folder in [Files](@guide:files), it compares the handler against what's really there and catches things like a misspelled file name or an executable that doesn't exist.

Every check has its own page with an example and the reasoning behind it, and [Every check](@site:rules/) lists them. If one fires on code that works fine in Nucleus, please tell us. The flag on the problem (**This check is wrong**) opens a report with the check and the line already filled in.

pages.title: Try it: what each player gets
pages.desc: See what each player would get, and test every combination.
pages.intro: Try it runs your handler once per player, the way Nucleus Co-op would, and shows what each player ends up with. That means the window, the launch arguments and every file change. You don't need Nucleus or the game for it, and it doesn't touch anything on your computer.

sections.md:
1. Open the **Try it** tab on the right or press {key:tryIt}.
2. Above the result, pick how many players there are, the monitor size, and who gets the keyboard and mouse.
3. Read through the player cards. Each one shows where the window goes, what the game is launched with, and which files get written or changed.

If the handler throws an error partway through, Try it shows where it happened and why. In Nucleus that's the point where the session would end.
A handler that works for two players can still break for three. **Test all combinations** ({key:testAll}) runs every player count, input setup and screen size, then lists the ones that fail and why.

Try it is a simulation. It emulates Jint, the JavaScript engine Nucleus uses, along with the handler API. File, registry and process calls are recorded and shown to you, but never carried out.

Where we weren't sure how Nucleus behaves, we ran small test handlers in the real engine. You can look at those under **Engine probes** in Advanced mode.
That would be a bug in Try it, and we'd like to hear about it. The icon in the corner of the result starts a report that puts what Try it showed next to what really happened.

pages.title: The debugger: step through a handler
pages.desc: Breakpoints, stepping forwards and back, and the variables for each player.
pages.intro: The debugger runs your handler one line at a time, player by player, so you can watch the variables change. It can also go backwards, which most debuggers can't.

sections.md:
1. Click next to a line number to put a breakpoint there. `F9` does the same for the line you're on.
2. In **Try it**, click **Step through** or press {key:debugGo}. The handler runs until it reaches the breakpoint.
3. `F10` runs the next line. If you went one too far, **Back** undoes the step.
4. The timeline covers every player's `Game.Play`. Drag it to jump around.

**Variables** shows the values at the current line. You can also see what the handler has done up to that point, such as the windows it placed and the files it changed.

Advanced mode adds a few things. You can watch an expression of your own, step into and out of functions, and put a condition on a breakpoint by right-clicking it, for example `Context.PlayerID == 1`.

pages.title: Open, save and files
pages.desc: Opening handlers and Hub packages, the Files panel, your game's folder, saving and sharing.
pages.intro: A handler is a .js file, often with a folder of extra files next to it. The workbench can open and save both, and it can save straight into your Nucleus Co-op folder.

sections.md:
Click the **+** next to the tabs or press {key:open}. From there you can start from a template, open one of the examples (the most downloaded verified Hub handlers are among them), search the Hub for a game, or open a file of your own. It reads .js, .zip and .nc files, and you can also drag a file onto the page.

Whatever you open gets its own tab.

The **Files** button above the code shows the whole package the way Nucleus installs it. You can open the text files in tabs and drop new files onto the panel. When you save, they go back into the package.

Under Files you'll find **Your game on this PC**. Point it at the folder your game is installed in, and Check will compare the handler's executable and file lists with the files that are really there. The folder is only read by your browser. Nothing gets uploaded.

- {key:save} saves a .zip, which is what Nucleus Co-op installs.
- The arrow beside **Save** (or {key:saveAs}) lets you pick .js or .nc instead. The .nc format is what the Hub uses.
- **Into Nucleus Co-op** writes the handler directly into the handlers folder. You choose the folder once. Firefox and Safari don't allow that, so there you get the .zip to drag onto Nucleus.
- **How to install it in Nucleus** walks you through installing it by hand.
**Share** sits next to Save. It copies a link to your handler, the code itself, or a code block formatted for Discord. If you select some lines first, it shares only those.

pages.title: AI in the workbench
pages.desc: Fix with AI, Explain with AI, AI-written docs, and using a chatbot or agent.
pages.intro: Nothing in the workbench needs AI. There are a few AI features, and they stay switched off until you set one up.

sections.md:
Once you've picked a provider under Settings › AI, a **Fix with AI** button shows up in Check. It's meant for the problems the automatic fixes can't handle. You get a before and after, and Undo if you don't like the result. You can use Claude, OpenAI, OpenRouter, Gemini, or a free local model through Ollama or LM Studio.

Your code is sent to that provider when you press the button, not before. API keys stay in your browser.
{key:explainLine} explains a line using the docs and Check, with no AI involved. If you have a provider set up, **Explain with AI** can add a longer answer. That answer is marked as AI-written.

The official docs don't cover every option. For the gaps, an AI wrote docs from the Nucleus source code. You can tell those parts by the tinted frame and the ✨ in the corner. Hover the sparkle to see what the text is based on, and use the 👍 or 👎 underneath to tell us whether it's right.

sections.h: Writing a handler with an AI
sections.md: If you're having ChatGPT, Claude, Codex or another AI write the handler, give it our prompt first. [Set up your AI](@site:ai/) has one for agents and one for chatbots. It teaches the AI the rules Nucleus has and makes it check its own work. Agents can go a step further and use the tools directly through the [MCP server](@docs:tools/mcp).

pages.title: Settings and looks
pages.desc: Themes, layout, Guided and Advanced mode, accessibility, and backing up your settings.
pages.intro: Settings is where you change how the workbench looks and how much it shows you. Open it from the menu or with {key:settings}. There's a search box at the top if you don't know where a setting lives.
shots: On a phone the code and the results take turns, and there's a row of symbol keys above the keyboard.

sections.md: In **Guided** mode you get tips and plainer wording. **Advanced mode**, which you switch on in the menu at the top right, is more compact and adds rule ids, filters, the recorded calls in Try it and the engine probes. You can flip between the two whenever you like.

Pick light, dark or whatever your device uses. There are four looks, including the original alpha 8 one and a Mac style, and the code can use the colours of GitHub, VS Code, Xcode, One, Monokai or Dracula. If none of that fits, download a look as a theme file, edit it and load it back.

The tools sit in a bar at the top by default. You can move them into a rail on the side, and put Files and Lines on either side of the code. Drag the edge between two panels to resize them, or right-click it for more options.
Nearly every shortcut can be changed under Settings › Keyboard shortcuts. [Shortcuts](@guide:shortcuts) has the full list, and pressing `?` in the workbench shows it too.

This section has colour-blind-friendly colours, a way to mark problems that doesn't rely on colour, a stronger focus ring, bigger buttons and an easier-to-read font. Notes can also be set to stay until you close them.
Settings › Updates and backup can export your settings to a file. Import that file in the other browser and you're set up the same way.

pages.title: Workbench shortcuts
pages.desc: Every keyboard shortcut in the workbench.
pages.intro: This is the workbench's own shortcut list. Press `?` in the workbench to see it there. You can change any of them under Settings › Keyboard shortcuts, apart from the ones marked *fixed*. Most match VS Code.
